title: Anthropic files to go public
excerpt: The company said Monday it has filed confidentially for an IPO.
dwp_take: Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, has filed confidential IPO paperwork with the SEC and is preparing to go public. This matters to digital workplace pros because generative AI is becoming embedded in every collaboration platform and productivity tool we support, and a major player's IPO signals these technologies aren't going anywhere. Here's the thing though: when AI companies go public, the pressure to monetize their tech intensifies, which usually means those "free tier" features your users love are about to get expensive real fast.

title: DuckDuckGo makes its ‘no-AI’ search engine easier to access as its traffic booms
excerpt: Alternative search engine DuckDuckGo launches 'no AI' web extensions for Chrome and Firefox users.
dwp_take: DuckDuckGo is rolling out browser extensions that let users search without AI-generated summaries cluttering up their results. This matters because it signals real demand from knowledge workers tired of AI slop polluting their search experience, which means your organization's search strategy needs to account for this backlash. Here's the thing though: if your employees are installing extensions to avoid AI results, you're probably already losing them to better tools elsewhere, so maybe don't force copilot summaries into your intranet search just yet.

title: Making sense of the debate over AI psychosis
excerpt: On the latest episode of Equity, we debate whether tech CEOs are "uniquely prone to AI psychosis."
dwp_take: Tech CEOs are apparently prone to making wild, unfounded claims about AI capabilities and timelines, leading to debate about whether this represents genuine delusion or just good marketing. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because these overblown narratives directly influence the AI tools you're actually expected to implement, often before they're ready for real work. Honestly, after three decades in this space, I've learned that the gap between what gets announced on stage and what actually works in your Slack channel is usually measured in years, not months.

title: ‘What a joke’: GitHub Copilot’s new token-based billing spurs consternation among devs
excerpt: The golden age of Microsoft's GitHub Copilot appears to be at an end.
dwp_take: GitHub switched Copilot from a seat-based subscription model to token-based billing, where developers pay for actual usage instead of a flat monthly fee. This matters because it signals how AI tools are shifting toward consumption-based pricing, which digital workplace leaders need to factor into their tech budgets and procurement strategies. The real irony is that Microsoft convinced everyone AI was going to make us more productive, then figured out they could charge us by the keystroke for that productivity gain, which is peak tech industry move.

title: New PC? This MX Linux version is the best distro for you
excerpt: MX Linux has released a version that includes certain features and software that make it a brilliant option for computers that are 1-3 years old.
dwp_take: MX Linux dropped a new version optimized for older hardware, specifically machines between one and three years old. Here's the thing though: if your organization is still standardizing on Windows, this distro is interesting for personal projects but won't solve your real problem, which is that nobody wants to retrain their workforce on Linux just to squeeze another year out of a laptop.

title: Chrome stops hackers from stealing your browser cookies now - how its new security feature works
excerpt: Now available for all Windows users, Chrome's security feature will thwart attackers who try to impersonate you by using your stolen browser cookies on their own devices.
dwp_take: Google Chrome added a security feature that prevents attackers from using stolen cookies to impersonate you on different devices, now rolling out to all Windows users. This matters because workplace browsers handle authentication tokens for email, cloud storage, and internal systems, so cookie theft is a real threat to corporate security posture. Finally, someone remembered that "just asking nicely" and "hoping nobody notices" aren't viable security strategies, though I'd love to see Microsoft follow suit with Edge before we're all here again in 2026.

title: 14 high-achiever habits that lead straight to burnout
excerpt: High achievers often mistake their most productive habits for the very behaviors driving them toward burnout. This article draws on insights from workplace psychology experts and organizational leader
dwp_take: Fast Company identified fourteen high-achiever habits that paradoxically drive burnout, from overcommitment to perfectionism to inability to delegate. This matters because digital workplace leaders often inadvertently design cultures that reward exactly these behaviors through always-on collaboration tools, endless meeting culture, and metrics that punish time off. Here's the thing though: knowing that perfectionism causes burnout doesn't stop perfectionists from burning out, so the real question is whether your organization will actually change incentives or just add a wellness webinar to the calendar.

title: Everyone wants to kill the middle manager role. The data says don’t do it
excerpt: Recently, I spoke with a head of HR for a tech company who asked: “Are you hearing of other organizations eliminating the manager role? Our CEO thinks they won’t be needed in the future because of AI,
dwp_take: A new Fast Company piece pushes back on the trend of eliminating middle managers, arguing the data shows they're still essential even as AI and self-managing teams gain traction. This matters because digital workplace leaders are often caught between executive hype about flattening org structures and the messy reality that humans still need coordination, feedback, and someone to actually make decisions. The irony is thick: CEOs who want to eliminate middle managers are literally the people those managers protect them from having to deal with directly.

Here's the thing though: I've watched people spend more time reading procrastination books than they would have spent just doing the actual work in the first place.

title: The hidden gap between how others see you and what you’re worth
excerpt: The biggest career risk right now isn’t being replaced by AI. It’s being misunderstood by humans. A senior partner at a global consulting firm recently described to me what she thought she was experie
dwp_take: A senior consulting partner realized her actual track record of major restructurings and industry pivots didn't match how her organization perceived her value, which she initially mistook for imposter syndrome. Digital workplace professionals need to understand this gap because remote work, async communication, and organizational silos make visibility harder than ever, meaning your accomplishments literally don't exist if nobody sees them. The real career threat isn't AI or layoffs, it's being invisible in your own company, which is why documenting your work and over-communicating wins across platforms matters more than pretending you're doing fine.
